question:
(a) The radius of a nucleus is $R = R_{0}A^{1/3}$. Calculate the radius of a nucleus having $A = 64$, taking $R_{0} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{m}$.
(b) If another nucleus has mass number $A = 8$, compare their radii.
(c) Justify the result physically.

options.A:
(a) $R_{64}=1.2\times10^{-15}\times64=7.68\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{m}$.
(b) $R_{64}:R_8=8:1$.
(c) Radius increases directly with mass number.
options.B:
(a) $R_{64}=1.2\times10^{-15}\times64^{1/3}=1.2\times10^{-15}\times4=4.8\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$.
(b) $R_{64}/R_8=(64/8)^{1/3}=2$, so the $A=64$ nucleus has twice the radius.
(c) Radius varies as $A^{1/3}$, so an eightfold increase in $A$ doubles the radius.
options.C:
(a) $R_{64}=1.2\times10^{-15}/4=3.0\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm{m}$.
(b) Both radii are equal.
(c) Radius does not depend on mass number.
